dataIdentification.abstract:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
dataIdentification.purpose: Land cover  is extremely important for natural resource assessment and management, environmental modeling and decision-making. Given that the Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) global dataset on land cover, the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme has promoted the processing of this database to make it complaints with the GLCN standards and usable through its tools set for land cover based analysis and modelling.

lineage.statement: This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Country Guidelines for the GSNmap initiative (FAO, 2022), which provide technical specifications for generating national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. The guidelines describe standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions, with outputs including soil nutrient levels as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity. These products support evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en

citation.title: Longest period of consecutive dry days in temperature (Global - 20 years average - ~10 km) - GAEZ v5

dataIdentification.abstract:
The longest period of consecutive dry days in temperature (growing period LGPt=5) dataset is provided at approximately 10 km spatial resolution globally, using different climate data sources for both historical and future periods.

Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020.

For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.

The longest period of consecutive dry days in temperature dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Resources theme and Growing Period sub-theme.

For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

citation.title: Land cover (Cote d'Ivoire - 2005 - 300 m) - Globcover Regional

dataIdentification.abstract:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
dataIdentification.purpose: Land cover  is extremely important for natural resource assessment and management, environmental modeling and decision-making. Given that the Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) global dataset on land cover, the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme has promoted the processing of this database to make it complaints with the GLCN standards and usable through its tools set for land cover based analysis and modelling.

lineage.statement: This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

citation.title: Hazards risk component (Global - Baseline) - CRTB

dataIdentification.abstract:
Historical climate data are an ensemble of outputs from CMIP6 earth system models for the time period 1981-2010.


The data from each original layer is divided into 4 categories contributing to the overall climate risk, based on a quantile method or manual break. A Metadata document containing information on the original data for each individual layer can be downloaded through the platform and visualized through the Climate Risk Toolbox – Guiding material for climate risk screening.

**Baseline hazards layers**

- Dry days: annual number of days with precipitation < 1mm


- Extreme high temperatures: annual number of days with Tmax > 35ºC.


- Extreme precipitation: annual maximum 1-day precipitation (mm). 


- Ocean temperatures: annual average sea surface temperatures (ºC).


- Ocean acidification: average pH at sea surface level.

organization.description: The Climate Risk Toolbox – CRTB was developed by the FAO Risks Team (FAO Environment Workstream within the FAO Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment – OCB) and the FAO AgroInformatics Team (FAO Digitalization and Informatics – CSI Division) to support the design of climate-resilient agricultural investment projects and plans, by allowing users to conduct climate risk screenings through advanced climate-related geospatial information and data. The CRTB is built on top of the FAO Hand-in-Hand (HiH) Geospatial Platform, which provides open-access geographic information, key food security indicators and agricultural statistics sourced from FAO and from external organizations such as NGOs, academia, the private sector, and space agencies, unlocking over 2 million data layers for more targeted, evidence-based interventions. The HiH platform is developed and scaled up by the FAO AgroInformatics team of the Digitalization and Informatics Division.

notes:
Historical climate data are an ensemble of outputs from CMIP6 earth system models for the time period 1981-2010.


The data from each original layer is divided into 4 categories contributing to the overall climate risk, based on a quantile method or manual break. A Metadata document containing information on the original data for each individual layer can be downloaded through the platform and visualized through the Climate Risk Toolbox – Guiding material for climate risk screening.

**Baseline hazards layers**

- Dry days: annual number of days with precipitation < 1mm


- Extreme high temperatures: annual number of days with Tmax > 35ºC.


- Extreme precipitation: annual maximum 1-day precipitation (mm). 


- Ocean temperatures: annual average sea surface temperatures (ºC).


- Ocean acidification: average pH at sea surface level.

citation.title: UCL-Forest Classification (DR Congo)

dataIdentification.abstract:
Based on: A. Verhegghen, P. Defourny, "A new 300 m vegetation map for Central Africa based on multi-sensor times series", Third Recent Advance in Quantitative Remote Sensing, J.A. Sobrino (Ed.), Publicaciones de la Universitat de Valencia,Valencia, Spain, 2010.608
Vegetation types of 8 countries in Central Africa have been mapped thanks to a semi-automatic processing method based on temporal and spectral information from 19 months of ENVISAT MERIS FRS observation and 8 years of SPOT VEGETATION time series. The approach is based on a previous 1-km mapping effort for the Democratic Republic of Congo and on the lessons learnt from the ESA-GlobCover project. A land cover map with 20 vegetation classes was produced in five major steps: data compositing, seasonal stratification of the study zone, unsupervised classifications, automatic labelling and manual editing. The floristic composition and physiognomy of each vegetation type are described using the Land Cover Classification System developed by the FAO. This mapping exercise will be a reference document to deliver area estimates of the different forest types in a consistent way for DRCongo, Gabon, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Central African Republic, Congo, Rwanda and Burundi.
For the display of the NFMS portal, the original data has been reprojected to "latlong" projection, cropped, and masked for the area of the DRC.

**FAO at the front line of monitoring forests and ecosystems**

FAO has supported more than 50 countries in their development of robust National Forest Monitoring Systems (NFMS), with the goal of developing reliable forest resource information for creating national forest policies, planning, and sustainable development, based on the affirmation that better data leads to better decisions. Forest monitoring systems include measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) functions and aim to produce high-quality, reliable data on forests, including forest-carbon estimates, that are critical in the battle against climate change.

More information can be found at https://www.fao.org/national-forest-monitoring/areas-of-work/en/

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Country Guidelines for the GSNmap initiative (FAO, 2022), which provide technical specifications for generating national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. The guidelines describe standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions, with outputs including soil nutrient levels as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity. These products support evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

citation.title: Predicted crop yield of maize and rice (Ecuador – 2025 – 10 km) - EOSTAT

dataIdentification.abstract:
This raster dataset provides an estimation of maize and rice yield in Ecuador for the year 2025, under a normal, wet, dry, hot and cold weather scenarios. Yield is expressed in Kilograms/Hectare.

Yield prediction is based on weather data from the NASA POWER dataset, which provides historical weather information. To forecast yields, an algorithm identifies past extreme weather events and classifies years into categories such as wet, dry, hot, cold, and normal, using 44 years of historical data (as of 2024).
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
No data value: -999

Unit : kg/ha

Scale Factor : 1.0

Map code : CRP-YLD-ECU

otherConstraints: This work is made available under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC-BY-4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

lineage.statement:
1) Methodology: SALUS (System Approach to Land Use Sustainability) model is used to predict crop yield. SALUS is a process-based crop simulation model that predicts yield by simulating crop growth, soil conditions, water and nutrient conditions under different management strategies for multiple years. 

2) Preprocessing:  Soil data is obtained from soil grid dataset is downscaled form 250m to 10km to strike a balance between maintaining high resolution and optimizing simulation computing time. NASA Power  data was used for its reliable and regular updates, as well as the consistency of its precipitation and temperature trends. SALUS Model calibration was conducted for selected crops using observed field data and/or peer-reviewed scientific literature, depending on availability. For example, empirical data from international studies were used to calibrate crops such as cocoa, sugar cane, and potato. For other crops like maize, precalibrated crop parameters from existing SALUS configurations were used. 

3) In-situ: Insitu data was used coming from the The Ministry of agriculture and livestock (MAG) for the year 2023. 

4) Validation: Maize and Rice  yield simulated and expected for Peru had a relative percentage error (RPE) of 15.9% and 11.2% respectively.

citation.title: Landslide (Baseline)

dataIdentification.abstract:
Landslide: areas where median annual rainfall-triggered landslide is above 0. Pixels with a value higher than the specified threshold (0) were given a value of 1 (YES response)

organization.description:
The Land and Water Division (NSL) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has developed a platform to support global and national-level drought monitoring. The global platform provides access to curated datasets and analytical tools designed to characterize drought vulnerability.  The platform integrates authoritative datasets across a people, land, and water framework, enabling governments, development practitioners, financial institutions, and research communities to identify drought-prone areas, assess risk, and prioritize targeted responses. The tool is intended to serve as part of an iterative process of drought monitoring, response, and mitigation.  The methodology is globally consistent while allowing for country-specific contextualization to reflect local conditions and needs.
Datasets span four key vulnerability dimensions (environmental, infrastructure, economic, and social) and are relevant to sectors including water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), agriculture & livestock, energy, environment, and inland navigation. They are available for viewing and download on an individual basis. In addition, analytic tools are available to collectively assess vulnerability across dimensions and datasets.
Developed in collaboration with CIMA Research Foundation.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The Global Soil Nutrient and Nutrient Budget Maps (GSNmap) is an initiative under the Global Soil Partnership that provides national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. Following the Country Guidelines (https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en ), it uses standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions. Outputs include soil nutrient as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity, supporting evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development.

This particular dataset was produced under the SOIL+ project, sponsored by the Asian Food and Agriculture Cooperation Initiative (AFACI, https://www.rda.go.kr/afaci/site/project/view?). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GloSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

citation.title: Overall climate risks (SSP5-8.5 - Near-term: 2021-2040)

dataIdentification.abstract: To produce the following climate risk maps, the different components of risk (hazard, exposure and vulnerability) are aggregated based on the IPCC definition of risk (IPCC-AR5, 2014). The risk of climate related impacts results from the interaction of climatological, hydrological and meteorological hazards (including climate extremes and climate variability) with the exposure of human and natural systems, including agriculture, together with livelihoods´ vulnerability. In addition, changes in both the climate system and socioeconomic processes include adaptation and mitigation measures, which are drivers of hazards, exposure and vulnerability. Although mitigation of climate hazards is not considered in the computation of climate risks, the modulation of risks is carefully included, commonly implemented through adaptive responses and often integrated within existing programs/policies related to disaster risk management by (i) preventing new disaster risk, (ii) reducing existing disaster risk and managing residual risk, and (iii) contributing to the strengthening of climate resilience and reduction of disaster losses. As a result, we obtain a set of maps that consider the overall climate risk for the baseline period, near-term (2021-40) and mid-term (2041-60), respectively for a low emission scenario (SSP1-2.6) and a high emission scenario (SSP5-8.5).

Further disaggregation is possible using land cover classes, exclusion layers, and agro-ecological zoning classes as defined in GAEZ v5.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The length of crop growth cycle (days) dataset is provided at approximately 10 km spatial resolution globally, using different climate data sources for both historical and future periods.

Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020.

For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Potential Yield theme and Growth Cycle Attributes sub-theme.

Please note that modeled results for crop sub-types are available only via download from Google Cloud Storage and are not published on the GAEZ v5 platform. For additional information on the data contained in this dataset, please see the [(readme file)](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/65971839-d0ad-4ada-8d64-17f90f90f537/resource/f95a7517-b561-4031-94dd-db4d317e044e/download/_readme_res02.xlsx).

For more detail on the GAEZ v5 methodology, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Potential Yield theme and Growth Cycle Attributes sub-theme.

Please note that modeled results for crop sub-types are available only via download from Google Cloud Storage and are not published on the GAEZ v5 platform. For additional information on the data contained in this dataset, please see the [(readme file)](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/65971839-d0ad-4ada-8d64-17f90f90f537/resource/f95a7517-b561-4031-94dd-db4d317e044e/download/_readme_res02.xlsx).

dataIdentification.abstract:
Results on soil quality (SQ) for agricultural production are mapped at an approximate spatial resolution of 1 km. Each grid cell is classified according to the level of soil or terrain constraint affecting land suitability.

The assessment is based on soil and terrain attributes from the Harmonized World Soils Database version 2.01 (HWSD v2.01; FAO & IIASA. 2023) and processed through the Global Agro-Ecological Zoning v5 (GAEZ) framework. Soil suitability is determined through crop-specific evaluations of seven major soil qualities relevant to agriculture:

- SQ1: Nutrient availability
- SQ2: Nutrient retention capacity
- SQ3: Rooting conditions
- SQ4: Oxygen availability for roots
- SQ5: Presence of salinity and sodicity
- SQ6: Presence of lime and gypsum
- SQ7: Workability

Soil qualities have been estimated for the dominant soils in each grid cell, using maize as the reference crop. 
Each soil quality is evaluated by comparing soil attributes against crop-specific requirements under different input and management levels. Results are expressed as normalized ratings ranging from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates no constraint and lower values represent increasing levels of limitation to potential productivity. The GAEZ methodology integrates these ratings into a soil index using a multiplicative aggregation procedure. The final classification identifies the most limiting factor in each grid cell, considering both soil and slope conditions.

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Land and Water Resources theme and Soil Resources sub-theme.

For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Global Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration Potential Map (GSOCseq), developed under the Global Soil Partnership to support Sustainable Development Goal Indicator 15.3 on land degradation neutrality. The GSOCseq map follows a country-driven bottom-up approach, where national SOC sequestration maps are produced and validated by local experts using standardized SOC models and the best available data. These products provide an evidence base for assessing soil restoration potential and supporting sustainable land management policies. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cb2642en

dataIdentification.abstract:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
dataIdentification.purpose: Land cover  is extremely important for natural resource assessment and management, environmental modeling and decision-making. Given that the Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) global dataset on land cover, the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme has promoted the processing of this database to make it complaints with the GLCN standards and usable through its tools set for land cover based analysis and modelling.

lineage.statement: This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

resources.description:
The Land Cover Legend Registry (LCLR) provides access to available land cover legends used to describe land cover. The description of the land cover classes have been extracted from the original documents. Several of them were prepared using LCCS.v2 and/or LCCS.v3 tool. LCCS.v3 was developed to prepare land cover legends and applying the Land Cover Meta Language (LCML), an ISO standard (ISO 19144-2:2012). LCCS.v3 is a user-friendly metadata tool, with a graphical user-friendly interface (not a reference classification system) that allows the classification of the land cover features in a comprehensive system, applying the LCML standard. When available, the link to the land cover map on FAO Map Catalog and FAO HiH is provided.

The structure of a set of registers and an associated registry for the description of the Land Cover legends used by the UN FAO and associated other organizations is based on the registry concepts identified in ISO 19144-1 and makes use of the descriptive metalanguage described in ISO 19144-2.

LCLR provides access to:
- A list of LC datasets held by the FAO or associated organizations. 
- A list of the available LCL (or schema) that are used within these LC datasets and 
- A list of LCL classes used within these legends.

Land cover (LC) information has been playing an important role in the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Maintaining and restoring land resources can play a vital task in tackling climate change, securing biodiversity and maintaining crucial ecosystem services, while ensuring resilient livelihoods and food security. Therefore, assessing LC is essential and is one of the 14 fundamental geospatial data themes of the United Nations according to United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM).
 
In this context, there are many different Land Cover Legend (LCL) and LC classification schemes used to classify LC. However, in many practical situations, the rigidity / vagueness of traditional LC classifications based on names and relative text description limits the interoperability between LCL and contribute to the inconsistency of LC information at regional and global levels. Therefore, there is a need to develop a platform with updated LC datasets along with harmonized LCL to address regional and worldwide land monitoring requirements and environmental issues. 

As a part of this effort, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has developed a Land Cover Legend Registry (LCLR). This open source web-catalogue is the first world’s largest repository of harmonized national, regional, and global LC legends with detailed information of LCL class and is linked with original LC datasets.

citation.title: Land cover (Comoros - 2005 - 300 m) - Globcover Regional

dataIdentification.abstract:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
dataIdentification.purpose: Land cover  is extremely important for natural resource assessment and management, environmental modeling and decision-making. Given that the Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) global dataset on land cover, the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme has promoted the processing of this database to make it complaints with the GLCN standards and usable through its tools set for land cover based analysis and modelling.

lineage.statement: This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

citation.title: Percentage of irrigated area serviced by groundwater (Global - 8 km)

dataIdentification.abstract:
This grid map at around 8 km resolution shows the percentage of irrigated area supplied by groundwater. Irrigation mainly relies on renewable freshwater resources, either surface water or groundwater. However, while the extent of irrigation and related water uses are reported in statistical databases or by model simulations, information on the source of irrigation water is still very rare. The map was compiled to support the analysis of SOLAW report concerning trends and current use of water use in agriculture, 

A global inventory undertaken by FAO and the University of Bonn reports that 113 million ha, or 38 percent of the total area equipped for irrigation of 301 million ha, is irrigated by groundwater (Siebert et al, 2010).

otherConstraints: This work is made available under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license (CC-BY-4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

dataIdentification.purpose: The map is part of the SOLAW Report to support the analysis concerning trends and current use of water in agriculture.

lineage.statement:

- Global map of irrigation areas at 5 arc-min (Siebert et al., 2007)

- Data on sources of irrigation water available by country through the FAO AQUASTAT database

- Additional data obtained through desk studies on distribution of sources of irrigation water. 

The legend indicates the share of irrigated land serviced by groundwater in each pixel.

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

name: 8613bce1-638b-43c4-987d-7da8d5aa27e2
notes:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)



	
**Data creation:** 2022-12-13
	



**Supplemental Information:**

This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
 
	






	
**Contact points:**

Resource Contact: [Antonio Martucci](mailto:Antonio.Martucci@fao.org)
				
			
		
			
			
			
			
			
		
			
			
			
			
			
		
			
			
			
			
			
		
			
			
			
			
			
		
			
			
			
			
			
		
			
			
			
			
			
		
	




**Data lineage:**

This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

dataIdentification.abstract:
Crop suitability index in classes, all land in grid cell for wheat, cotton and sugarcane under rain-fed conditions and high input level, with and without CO2 fertilization, using different climate data source and based on different Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) according to the time period as follows:
- climate data source CRUTS32 based on historical data for the time period 1981-2010;
- climate data source ENSEMBLE based on the Representative Concentration Pathway RCP8.5 for time period 2041-2070.

The Crop suitability index in classes dataset is part of the GAEZ v4 Theme 4 Suitability and Attainable Yield, Suitability Class sub-theme.

For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v4 Model Documentation.

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

citation.title: Clay texture fraction (Laos - 250 m) - GSNmap v2026

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Country Guidelines for the GSNmap initiative (FAO, 2022), which provide technical specifications for generating national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. The guidelines describe standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions, with outputs including soil nutrient levels as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity. These products support evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

dataIdentification.abstract:
Results on production for the year 2020 are expressed as tonnes and provided at a global scale with approximately 10 km spatial resolution for 38 major crops/crop groups  [(see Appendix 4-1 of the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation)](https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki/14.-Appendix-4%E2%80%901-Crops), separately in rain-fed, irrigated or total cropland. Country totals are based on FAOSTAT statistics for the years 2019-2021 (accessed in 2022).

For single crops or fairly homogenous crop groups (other cereals, yams and other roots) the units of production are in 1000 tonnes (as used in FAOSTAT). For crop groups which include a greater variety of crops (i.e., vegetables, stimulants) international price weights compiled by FAO (constant 2014-2016 I$) were used to aggregate individual items.

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Actual Yields and Production theme and Area, Yield and Production sub-theme.

For additional information on the data contained in this dataset, please see the [(readme file)](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/6b9e59f6-89be-46a1-a62b-1d1d16450a1c/resource/92187c2b-b32d-4185-bc26-d3a3c83b7f00/download/_readme_res06.xlsx). organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The Digital Soil Map of the World is a global vector dataset based on the original [FAO-UNESCO World Soil Map](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/iso/cc45a270-88fd-11da-a88f-000d939bc5d8), published in 10 volumes and 19 cartographic sheets from 1972 to 1977.

The digitized soil map, in geographic projection (latitude - longitude) and at a scale of 1:5,000,000, was intersected with a layer containing hydrographic features (coasts, lakes, glaciers, and dual-course rivers) and, with the exception of the African continent, with the map of national boundaries obtained from the World Data Bank II (United States Government) updated in January 1994 at a scale of 1:3,000,000. For Africa, national boundaries were derived from the boundaries of the Original FAO/UNESCO World Soil Map of the World. In both cases, national boundaries have been verified and, where necessary, adjusted based on FAO and UN conventions.

The Digital Soil Map of the World in PDF and GIS formats is available for download in the **Data and Resources** section of this metadata. Maps and legends can be also found on the [**FAO Soil Portal**](http://www.fao.org/soils-portal/soil-survey/soil-maps-and-databases/faounesco-soil-map-of-the-world/en/), along with the related reports, for the following regions: North America, Mexico and Central America, South America, Europe, Asia, South Asia, North and Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and Australasia.

organization.description: The Climate Risk Toolbox – CRTB was developed by the FAO Risks Team (FAO Environment Workstream within the FAO Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment – OCB) and the FAO AgroInformatics Team (FAO Digitalization and Informatics – CSI Division) to support the design of climate-resilient agricultural investment projects and plans, by allowing users to conduct climate risk screenings through advanced climate-related geospatial information and data. dataIdentification.abstract:
Agro-ecological attainable yield results are represented as the output density (potential production divided by total grid cell area), expressed as Kg (DW)/ha, with a spatial resolution of approximately 1 km. They account for both rain-fed and irrigated conditions, as well as two different levels of input management (high and low). Results are provided for more than 70 major crops including traditional and adapted crops in alignment with the Vision for Adapted Crops and Soils (VACS) [(see Appendix 4-1 of the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation)](https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki/14.-Appendix-4%E2%80%901-Crops), and cover all land and soil groups identified in the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD v2) (FAO & IIASA, 2023). Note, results for irrigated cultivation are limited to grid cells where existing cropland is indicated in the GAEZ v5 land cover inventory for 2020.

For most crops the yields are given in kg dry weight per hectare. For sugar beet and sugar cane the yields are in kg sugar per hectare and for oil palm in kg oil per hectare. Cotton yields are given as kg lint per hectare. Note that for comparison of statistical production (usually in harvested/fresh weight) with GAEZ simulated potential production (yield calculated mostly as dry weight of main produce) an appropriate conversion factor must be applied. Technical coefficients used to convert to fresh weight are included in the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation.

Agro-ecological attainable yield  is estimated using different climate data sources for both historical and future periods.
Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020.
For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.c Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Suitability and Attainable Yield theme and Suitability Index sub-theme.

For additional information on the data contained in this dataset, please see the [(readme file)](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/6d2d9493-411e-4e58-bc9f-8164dd3a7524/resource/ee50561e-9d71-4397-8f51-960dd92b566e/download/_readme_res05.xlsx). organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

dataIdentification.abstract:
**Geographic information – Classification systems: Land Use Meta Language (LUML)**

**Part 3: ISO 19144-3:2024 (Edition 1)**

The ISO 19144-3 – land use meta language (LUML) was prepared jointly by FAO, Technical Committee of ISO i.e., Technical Committee 211 (TC211) on Geographic information/Geomatics, and European Committee for Standardization (CEN) Technical Committee CEN/TC 287. 

This document specifies a Land Use Meta Language (LUML) expressed as a UML metamodel that allows different land use classification systems to be described. This document recognizes that there are a number of land use classification systems in existence. It provides a common reference structure for the comparison and integration of data for any generic land use classification system, but does not intend to replace those classification systems. This document complements ISO 19144-2 on Land Cover Meta Language (LCML) and can be used independently to describe land use or together with ISO 19144-2 to describe a combined land cover land use.FAO acknowledges with deep appreciation the exceptional permission granted by ISO to continue republishing the current editions of the ISO 19144 series as FAO publications. This unique arrangement underscores the spirit of mutual trust and collaboration between the two organizations, ensuring wider and equitable access to these essential standards by Member Nations, technical partners and practitioners around the world.

citation.title: Geographic information – Classification systems: Land Use Meta Language (LUML)

dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This is part of the ISO 19144 standard series, jointly developed by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO).

The ISO 19144 series offer a globally consistent and interoperable framework for land cover and land use data. Through a unified structure (ISO 19144-1), a Land Cover Meta Language (ISO 19144-2), and a Land Use Meta Language (ISO 19144-3), these standards guide countries, organizations and experts to document land cover and land use classification systems, ensure connectivity between systems, interoperability between datasets, and improve consistency for reporting among many other applications and needs.

Recognizing land as a key enabler for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), these standards contribute to a wide range of applications—from agricultural to forest monitoring, from disaster risk to environmental assessments, from the local to global levels.

Under the auspice of the ISO/TC211 and the Advisory Group 13 on Land Cover Land Use, this achievement represents a major milestone in advancing land cover and land use semantic interoperability and supports the broader goals of integrated geospatial data governance at national, regional, and international levels.

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

organization.description: The Climate Risk Toolbox – CRTB was developed by the FAO Risks Team (FAO Environment Workstream within the FAO Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment – OCB) and the FAO AgroInformatics Team (FAO Digitalization and Informatics – CSI Division) to support the design of climate-resilient agricultural investment projects and plans, by allowing users to conduct climate risk screenings through advanced climate-related geospatial information and data. The CRTB is built on top of the FAO Hand-in-Hand (HiH) Geospatial Platform, which provides open-access geographic information, key food security indicators and agricultural statistics sourced from FAO and from external organizations such as NGOs, academia, the private sector, and space agencies, unlocking over 2 million data layers for more targeted, evidence-based interventions. notes: Water productivity is defined as the quantity or value of output in relation to the quantity of water beneficially consumed to produce this output. Water productivity in agriculture can be expressed as amount of product (biomass or yield, expressed in kg/ha) per unit of water consumed by the crop (evapotranspiration, in m³/ha). Remote sensing provides cost effective ways to help monitoring water productivity and, through spatially explicit outputs, it informs on variations, gaps and opportunities for closing productivity gaps in irrigation areas.

citation.title: Major agricultural systems (Global)

dataIdentification.abstract:
This map builds upon work done by Dixon (Dixon et al., 2001) in an attempt to propose a general classification of major farming systems. Based on a combination of global dataset, the map proposes a harmonized classification of major agricultural systems used as the basis for the analysis of SOLAW's Systems at risk. The map is based on an interpretation of global land cover data, combined with thematic datasets showing irrigated land and paddy rice extent.

The map is published in SOLAW Report: The state of the world's land and water resources for food and agriculture - Managing systems at risk (2011) and SOLAW Thematic Report 15: Sustainable options for addressing land and water problems - a problem tree and case studies (links in the online resources section).

citation.title: Mean annual precipitation (Global - 20 years average - ~10 km) - GAEZ v5

dataIdentification.abstract:
The mean annual precipitation dataset is provided at approximately 10 km spatial resolution globally, using different climate data sources for both historical and future periods.

Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020.

For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.

The reference actual evapotranspiration dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Resources theme and Moisture Regime sub-theme.

For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

organization.description:
The Land and Water Division (NSL) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has developed a platform to support global and national-level drought monitoring. The global platform provides access to curated datasets and analytical tools designed to characterize drought vulnerability.  The platform integrates authoritative datasets across a people, land, and water framework, enabling governments, development practitioners, financial institutions, and research communities to identify drought-prone areas, assess risk, and prioritize targeted responses. The tool is intended to serve as part of an iterative process of drought monitoring, response, and mitigation.  The methodology is globally consistent while allowing for country-specific contextualization to reflect local conditions and needs.
Datasets span four key vulnerability dimensions (environmental, infrastructure, economic, and social) and are relevant to sectors including water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), agriculture & livestock, energy, environment, and inland navigation. They are available for viewing and download on an individual basis. In addition, analytic tools are available to collectively assess vulnerability across dimensions and datasets.
Developed in collaboration with CIMA Research Foundation.

citation.title: OCSeq Relative sequestration rate sustainable soil management 3 (Cambodia - 1 km) - GSOCSeq v2021

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Global Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration Potential Map (GSOCseq), developed under the Global Soil Partnership to support Sustainable Development Goal Indicator 15.3 on land degradation neutrality. The GSOCseq map follows a country-driven bottom-up approach, where national SOC sequestration maps are produced and validated by local experts using standardized SOC models and the best available data. These products provide an evidence base for assessing soil restoration potential and supporting sustainable land management policies. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cb2642en

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.
