organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

citation.title: Predicted crop yield of maize, potato, rice, and sugarcane (Peru - 2025 - 10 km) - EOSTAT

dataIdentification.abstract:
This raster dataset provides an estimation of maize, potato and rice, and sugarcane yield in Peru for the year 2025, under a normal, wet, dry, hot and cold weather scenarios. Yield is expressed in Kilograms/Hectare.

Yield prediction is based on weather data from the NASA POWER dataset, which provides historical weather information. To forecast yields, an algorithm identifies past extreme weather events and classifies years into categories such as wet, dry, hot, cold, and normal, using 44 years of historical data (as of 2024).
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
No data value: -999

Unit : kg/ha

Scale Factor : 1.0

Map code : CRP-YLD-PER

otherConstraints: This work is made available under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC-BY-4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

lineage.statement:
1) Methodology: SALUS (System Approach to Land Use Sustainability) model is used to predict crop yield. SALUS is a process-based crop simulation model that predicts yield by simulating crop growth, soil conditions, water and nutrient conditions under different management strategies for multiple years. 

2) Preprocessing:  Soil data is obtained from soil grid dataset is downscaled form 250m to 10km to strike a balance   between maintaining high resolution and optimizing simulation computing time. NASA Power  data was used for its reliable and regular updates, as well as the consistency of its precipitation and temperature trends. SALUS Model calibration was conducted for selected crops using observed field data and/or peer-reviewed scientific literature, depending on availability. For example, empirical data from international studies were used to calibrate crops such as cocoa, sugar cane, and potato. For other crops like maize, precalibrated crop parameters from existing SALUS configurations were used.

3) In-situ: In-situ data was used coming from the Peruvian government for the year 2021. 

4) Validation: Maize yield simulated and expected for Peru had a relative percentage error (RPE) of 15.9%, Rice 14.2%, Sugarcane 22.1% and Potato 28.9%.

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

citation.title: Combined suitability of currently available land for pasture and rainfed crops (high input level) (FGGD)

dataIdentification.abstract: The FGGD combined suitability maps at low, intermediate and high levels of inputs under rainfed conditions on currently available land are global raster datalayers with a resolution of 5 arc-minutes. Pixels classified as urban, closed forest or irrigated contain negative values. Each remaining pixel contains a combined suitability class value for rainfed agriculture, based on the 2005 version of the suitability indexes for rainfed production of all crops plus pasture. The method is described in FAO and IIASA, 2007, Mapping biophysical factors that influence agricultural production and rural vulnerability, by H. von Velthuizen et al.

notes:
The FGGD combined suitability maps at low, intermediate and high levels of inputs under rainfed conditions on currently available land are global raster datalayers with a resolution of 5 arc-minutes. Pixels classified as urban, closed forest or irrigated contain negative values. Each remaining pixel contains a combined suitability class value for rainfed agriculture, based on the 2005 version of the suitability indexes for rainfed production of all crops plus pasture. The method is described in FAO and IIASA, 2007, Mapping biophysical factors that influence agricultural production and rural vulnerability, by H. von Velthuizen et al.



	
**Data publication:** 2007-09-18
	



**Supplemental Information:**

This dataset is contained in Module 6 "Land productivity potential" of Food Insecurity, Poverty and Environment Global GIS Database (FGGD) (FAO, 2007).

dataIdentification.abstract:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
dataIdentification.purpose: Land cover  is extremely important for natural resource assessment and management, environmental modeling and decision-making. Given that the Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) global dataset on land cover, the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme has promoted the processing of this database to make it complaints with the GLCN standards and usable through its tools set for land cover based analysis and modelling.

lineage.statement: This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

citation.title: Hydrological basins in Central America

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset divides the Central American continent in major hydrological basins and their sub-basins.according to its hydrological characteristics. It was obtained by delineating drainage basin boundaries from hydrologically corrected elevation data (WWF HydroSHEDS and Hydro1K).

The dataset consists of the following information:- numerical code and name of the major basin (MAJ_BAS and MAJ_NAME); - area of the major basin in square km (MAJ_AREA); - numerical code and name of the sub-basin (SUB_BAS and SUB_NAME); - area of the sub-basin in square km (SUB_AREA); - numerical code of the sub-basin towards which the sub-basin flows (TO_SUBBAS) (the codes -888 and -999 have been assigned respectively to internal sub-basins and to sub-basins draining into the sea)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation: This dataset is developed as part of a GIS-based information system on water resources for the Central American continent. It has been published in the framework of the AQUASTAT - programme of the Land and Water Division of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.
dataIdentification.purpose: To assess which part of the land area flows to which river. The dataset is developed as part of an assessment of water resources in Central America.

lineage.statement: The linework of the map was obtained by delineating drainage basin boundaries from hydrologically corrected elevation data with a resolution of 15 arc-seconds.The elevation dataset was part of a mapping product, HydroSHEDS, developed by the Conservation Science Program of World Wildlife Fund.Original input data had been obtained during NASA's Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM).

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

organization.description: The Climate Risk Toolbox – CRTB was developed by the FAO Risks Team (FAO Environment Workstream within the FAO Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment – OCB) and the FAO AgroInformatics Team (FAO Digitalization and Informatics – CSI Division) to support the design of climate-resilient agricultural investment projects and plans, by allowing users to conduct climate risk screenings through advanced climate-related geospatial information and data. The CRTB is built on top of the FAO Hand-in-Hand (HiH) Geospatial Platform, which provides open-access geographic information, key food security indicators and agricultural statistics sourced from FAO and from external organizations such as NGOs, academia, the private sector, and space agencies, unlocking over 2 million data layers for more targeted, evidence-based interventions. The HiH platform is developed and scaled up by the FAO AgroInformatics team of the Digitalization and Informatics Division.

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

**Remote Sensing Based Water Productivity Assessment in Karaghandy selected schemes. Karaghandy, Kazakhstan**

The activities undertaken for Kazakhstan focused in the Karaghandy region, and were intended to support the proposed Irrigation Rehabilitation Sector Project which is being prepared as part of Kazakhstan Government’s “State Program on Development of Agricultural Industry for 2017-2021”. In the Karaghandy region the Project will finance rehabilitation of 6 canals and 23 pipelines in 10 schemes of 6 districts, namely Abai, Zhezkazgan, Zhanaarka, Bukhar-Zhyrau, Osakarovka and Nura districts.

**Downloads:**

citation.title: Hydrological basins in Europe

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset divides the European continent in major hydrological basins and their sub-basins according to its hydrological characteristics. It was obtained by delineating drainage basin boundaries from hydrologically corrected elevation data (WWF HydroSHEDS and Hydro1K).

The dataset consists of the following information:- numerical code and name of the major basin (MAJ_BAS and MAJ_NAME); - area of the major basin in square km (MAJ_AREA); - numerical code and name of the sub-basin (SUB_BAS and SUB_NAME); - area of the sub-basin in square km (SUB_AREA); - numerical code of the sub-basin towards which the sub-basin flows (TO_SUBBAS) (the codes -888 and -999 have been assigned respectively to internal sub-basins and to sub-basins draining into the sea)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation: This dataset is developed as part of a GIS-based information system on water resources for the European continent. It has been published in the framework of the AQUASTAT - programme of the Land and Water Division of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.
dataIdentification.purpose: To assess which part of the land area flows to which river. The dataset is developed as part of an assessment of water resources in Europe.

lineage.statement: The majority of thelinework of the map was obtained by delineating drainage basin boundaries from hydrologically corrected elevation data with a resolution of 15 arc-seconds.The elevation dataset was part of a mapping product, HydroSHEDS, developed by the Conservation Science Program of World Wildlife Fund.Original input data had been obtained during NASA's Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM).Areas north of the SRTM extent, 60 degrees N, were obtained by merging with the HYDRO1k basin layer.

This dataset divides the European continent in major hydrological basins and their sub-basins according to its hydrological characteristics. It was obtained by delineating drainage basin boundaries from hydrologically corrected elevation data (WWF HydroSHEDS and Hydro1K).

The dataset consists of the following information:- numerical code and name of the major basin (MAJ_BAS and MAJ_NAME); - area of the major basin in square km (MAJ_AREA); - numerical code and name of the sub-basin (SUB_BAS and SUB_NAME); - area of the sub-basin in square km (SUB_AREA); - numerical code of the sub-basin towards which the sub-basin flows (TO_SUBBAS) (the codes -888 and -999 have been assigned respectively to internal sub-basins and to sub-basins draining into the sea)



	
**Data publication:** 2021-12-15
	



**Supplemental Information:**

This dataset is developed as part of a GIS-based information system on water resources for the European continent. It has been published in the framework of the AQUASTAT - programme of the Land and Water Division of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

In total, 351 training samples were generated with the help of expert agronomics interpretation, supported by NDVI time series, seasonal spectral variability, and historical vegetation layers. Image segmentation was applied to derive homogeneous objects, from which spectral, textural, and geometric features were extracted. citation.title: Crop suitability, class index (Global - 20 years average - ~1 km) - GAEZ v5

dataIdentification.abstract:
Crop suitability results are presented as an index, calculated for all land area and classified into categories, on grids with a spatial resolution of approximately 1 km. Estimations account for respectively rain-fed and irrigated conditions, different time periods, as well as two different levels of inputs and management (high and low). Results are provided for more than 70 major crops including traditional and adapted crops in alignment with the Vision for Adapted Crops and Soils (VACS) [(see Appendix 4-1 of the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation)](https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki/14.-Appendix-4%E2%80%901-Crops), and cover all land and soil groups identified in the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD v2) (FAO & IIASA, 2023). Note, results for irrigated cultivation are limited to grid cells where existing cropland is indicated in the GAEZ v5 land cover inventory for 2020.

The crop suitability index represents the weighted sum of extents in different suitability classes, expressing the suitability make up of a grid cell as a number in the range of 0 to 100. The index results in a value of 100 when all land in a location is assessed as very suitable (VS) and in a value 0 when all land is not suitable (NS).

Crop suitability index results at 1 km are provided only for the historical period. Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020.

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Suitability and Attainable Yield theme and Suitability Class sub-theme.

For additional information on the data contained in this dataset, please see the [(readme file)](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/94c469f7-3352-457e-8025-9bae98982109/resource/e931467d-6c0e-4f26-af4c-c9c2a5bcf9c4/download/_readme_res05.xlsx). For more detail on the GAEZ v5 methodology, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Global Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration Potential Map (GSOCseq), developed under the Global Soil Partnership to support Sustainable Development Goal Indicator 15.3 on land degradation neutrality. The GSOCseq map follows a country-driven bottom-up approach, where national SOC sequestration maps are produced and validated by local experts using standardized SOC models and the best available data. These products provide an evidence base for assessing soil restoration potential and supporting sustainable land management policies. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cb2642en

notes:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Global Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration Potential Map (GSOCseq), developed under the Global Soil Partnership to support Sustainable Development Goal Indicator 15.3 on land degradation neutrality. The GSOCseq map follows a country-driven bottom-up approach, where national SOC sequestration maps are produced and validated by local experts using standardized SOC models and the best available data. These products provide an evidence base for assessing soil restoration potential and supporting sustainable land management policies. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cb2642en

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

citation.title: Seasonal P/PET ratio, winter period (Global - Annual - ~10 km) - GAEZ v5

dataIdentification.abstract:
The seasonal P/PET ratio time series dataset is provided at approximately 10 km spatial resolution globally, spanning from 1980 to 2022. Climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program.

In the GAEZ methodology, a moisture availability index is calculated for different periods: for year-round conditions; for 6-month periods (April to September, October to March), and for 3-month periods (January to March, April to June, July to September, and October to December). The indicators provide a general understanding of soil moisture conditions and of the level of water stress occurring overall and within certain periods of a year.

The seasonal P/PET time series dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Resources theme and Moisture Regime sub-theme.

For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

organization.description:
The Land and Water Division (NSL) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has developed a platform to support global and national-level drought monitoring. The global platform provides access to curated datasets and analytical tools designed to characterize drought vulnerability.  The platform integrates authoritative datasets across a people, land, and water framework, enabling governments, development practitioners, financial institutions, and research communities to identify drought-prone areas, assess risk, and prioritize targeted responses. The tool is intended to serve as part of an iterative process of drought monitoring, response, and mitigation.  The methodology is globally consistent while allowing for country-specific contextualization to reflect local conditions and needs.
Datasets span four key vulnerability dimensions (environmental, infrastructure, economic, and social) and are relevant to sectors including water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), agriculture & livestock, energy, environment, and inland navigation. They are available for viewing and download on an individual basis. In addition, analytic tools are available to collectively assess vulnerability across dimensions and datasets.
Developed in collaboration with CIMA Research Foundation.

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

The crop evaluation results under the Suitability and Attainable Yield theme of GAEZ v5 have been processed and tabulated using various utility tools to generate crop summary statistics. These standardized statistics provide country-level insights for each crop, summarizing suitable land areas, attainable yields, and potential production by suitability class: 

![list](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/a55c337e-f7e6-4d2f-aa8e-6d2199171c37/resource/63c5ade8-0b19-444e-87e8-696596d1efb5/download/cropsummarydata_variables.jpg)

More details on the classes of indicators used for the delineation of spatial entities in the tabulation, along with all variables and their corresponding abbreviations, are explained in the [__read me file__](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/a55c337e-f7e6-4d2f-aa8e-6d2199171c37/resource/7f50e64c-4fd7-40c6-9e34-ebe3f9f7a6b7/download/gaezv5_cropsummarydata_readme.xlsx).

The crop summary data can be filtered by country, crop, climate data source, Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), time period, water supply conditions, and input management level. Further disaggregation is possible using land cover classes, exclusion layers, and agro-ecological zoning classes as defined in GAEZ v5.

For more information about the data used for the tabulation of Module V outputs please consult the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki.

citation.title: Land cover (Mauritius - 2005 - 300 m) - Globcover Regional

dataIdentification.abstract:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
dataIdentification.purpose: Land cover  is extremely important for natural resource assessment and management, environmental modeling and decision-making. Given that the Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) global dataset on land cover, the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme has promoted the processing of this database to make it complaints with the GLCN standards and usable through its tools set for land cover based analysis and modelling.

lineage.statement: This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

citation.title: Snow and glaciers - GLC-SHARE

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset is a raster format GeoTIFF representing the percentage of density in each pixel of snow and glaciers. It 
is part of the Global Land Cover-SHARE (GLC-SHARE) database at the global level created by FAO, Land and Water Division in partnership and with contribution from various partners and institutions.

The snow and glaciers dataset includes any geographic area covered by snow or glaciers persistently for 10 months or more.
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
GLC-SHARE provides a set of major thematic land cover layers resulting by a combination of "best available" high resolution national, regional and/or sub-national land cover databases with the weighted average land cover information derived from large-scale available datasets. The database is produced with a resolution of 30 arc second (1km). The approach implemented is based on the utilization of the Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) and SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting) legend systems for the harmonization of the various global, regional and national land cover legends.
The major benefit of the GLC-SHARE product is its capacity to preserve the existing and available high resolution land cover information at the regional and country level obtained by spatial and multi-temporal source data, integrating them with the best synthesis of global datasets.

Preliminary validation campaign was performed using 1000 random points statistically distributed over each land cover classes.
The database is distributed in the following eleven layers, in raster format (GeoTIFF ), whose pixel values represent the percentage of density coverage in each pixel of the land cover type. The dominant layer, representing the value of the dominant land cover type, is also available along with a legend in LYR ESRI format. Finally, information on each layer's source is retrievable in sources layer, by joining the raster values with an Excel table.
01-Artificial Surfaces 
02-CropLand
03-Grassland
04-Tree Covered Area
05-Shrubs Covered Area
06-Herbaceous vegetation, aquatic or regularly flooded
07-Mangroves
08-Sparse vegetation
09-BareSoil
10-Snow and glaciers
11-Waterbodies

notes:
This dataset is a raster format GeoTIFF representing the percentage of density in each pixel of snow and glaciers. It 
is part of the Global Land Cover-SHARE (GLC-SHARE) database at the global level created by FAO, Land and Water Division in partnership and with contribution from various partners and institutions.

The snow and glaciers dataset includes any geographic area covered by snow or glaciers persistently for 10 months or more.





	
**Data creation:** 2024-07-17
	



**Supplemental Information:**

GLC-SHARE provides a set of major thematic land cover layers resulting by a combination of "best available" high resolution national, regional and/or sub-national land cover databases with the weighted average land cover information derived from large-scale available datasets. The database is produced with a resolution of 30 arc second (1km). The approach implemented is based on the utilization of the Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) and SEEA (System of Environmental-Economic Accounting) legend systems for the harmonization of the various global, regional and national land cover legends.
The major benefit of the GLC-SHARE product is its capacity to preserve the existing and available high resolution land cover information at the regional and country level obtained by spatial and multi-temporal source data, integrating them with the best synthesis of global datasets.

Preliminary validation campaign was performed using 1000 random points statistically distributed over each land cover classes.
The database is distributed in the following eleven layers, in raster format (GeoTIFF ), whose pixel values represent the percentage of density coverage in each pixel of the land cover type. The dominant layer, representing the value of the dominant land cover type, is also available along with a legend in LYR ESRI format. Finally, information on each layer's source is retrievable in sources layer, by joining the raster values with an Excel table.
01-Artificial Surfaces 
02-CropLand
03-Grassland
04-Tree Covered Area
05-Shrubs Covered Area
06-Herbaceous vegetation, aquatic or regularly flooded
07-Mangroves
08-Sparse vegetation
09-BareSoil
10-Snow and glaciers
11-Waterbodies

name: agricultural-stress-index-system-asis-fao-global-agricultural-drought-monitoring-system
notes:
![Image](https://storage.googleapis.com/810c63d8-3fde-4ecd-9882-14d62e3058be/static/sites/hih/crop/images/ot2401h_aC1_s1_g2_644x209.png)

# Agricultural Stress Index System (ASIS)

The **Agricultural Stress Index System (ASIS)** is a global crop monitoring and agricultural drought early warning system developed and operated by FAO. By combining expertise in Earth observation (EO), agronomy, agrometeorology, and land-use analysis with large-scale geospatial datasets, ASIS transforms complex remote sensing information into actionable insights for a wide range of users.

ASIS provides a suite of global indicators that have been updated and disseminated every 10 days since 2014. These products are available at a spatial resolution of 1 km and are supported by a historical archive dating back to 1984. The system received the Geospatial World Excellence Award in 2016 and was recognized as a Digital Public Good (DPG) in 2024.

ASIS is routinely used by FAO's Global Information and Early Warning System (GIEWS) to support global crop monitoring, food security assessments, and early warning activities. As a unique collection of multidimensional datasets spanning more than 40 years, ASIS also supports a wide range of climate, agricultural, and socio-economic analyses conducted by governments, research institutions, and development partners worldwide.

Beyond its global products, ASIS has been adapted and implemented in approximately 20 countries, where it supports ministries, national early warning systems, and technical agencies in monitoring drought impacts on crops and rangelands. The system strengthens national capacities for climate risk management, agricultural planning, and anticipatory action. National institutions are responsible for operating and maintaining the ASIS Country Tool, while FAO provides EO data services, technical support, and capacity development.

ASIS provides two categories of indicators: **seasonal indicators** and **non-seasonal indicators**.

## Seasonal Indicators

Seasonal indicators are specifically designed for agricultural drought detection during the growing season. They include:

- **Agricultural Stress Index (ASI)**, which identifies areas affected by severe agricultural drought.
- **Drought Intensity (DI)**, which classifies drought severity.
- **Weighted Mean Vegetation Health Index (wVHI)**, the underlying indicator from which ASI and DI are derived.

These indicators are generated from remotely sensed vegetation and land surface temperature data combined with information on agricultural cropping cycles derived from historical observations and a global crop mask. The resulting products highlight anomalous vegetation conditions and potential drought impacts in agricultural areas during active growing seasons.

ASIS distinguishes between two cropping seasons (**Season 1** and **Season 2**) and between **crop** and **grassland** areas. The crop mask currently used is the **FAO GLC-SHARE** global land cover database.

## Non-Seasonal Indicators

Non-seasonal indicators provide alternative measures of vegetation condition independent of cropping calendars. These include:

- **NDVI Anomaly**
- **Vegetation Condition Index (VCI)**
- **Vegetation Health Index (VHI)**

These indicators measure vegetation conditions relative to historical norms rather than absolute vegetation density. They can be used to identify areas where vegetation is performing better or worse than expected for a given location and time of year.

A high value indicates that vegetation is healthier or less stressed than is typically observed under normal conditions, while a low value suggests below-average vegetation performance and potentially elevated stress levels. For example, a high index value in a sparsely vegetated environment, such as a savannah, represents above-average vegetation conditions for that environment rather than dense or lush vegetation cover.

## Recommended Use

For agricultural monitoring purposes, users are encouraged to rely primarily on the seasonal indicators (**ASI**, **DI**, and **wVHI**), as these products incorporate crop phenology information and are specifically designed to assess agricultural drought.

Where significant discrepancies between seasonal indicators and local observations are identified, the differences may be related to limitations in the crop phenology data and/or crop mask used by the system. In such cases, users may wish to consult the non-seasonal vegetation indicators as complementary sources of information.

Additional guidance is available in the **FAQs** section of the GIEWS Earth Observation website.

## Data Sources

The indicators are derived from 10-day (**dekadal**) vegetation datasets generated from the **METOP-AVHRR** sensor at 1 km spatial resolution from 2007 onwards. Historical data for the 1984-2006 period were reconstructed from **NOAA-AVHRR** observations originally available at 16 km spatial resolution and subsequently downscaled to 1 km resolution.

## Access to Data and Services

ASIS operates on a 10-day production cycle, delivering pre-processed, publication-ready maps and zonal statistics through the FAO [GIEWS Earth Observation website].(https://www.fao.org/giews/earthobservation/index.jsp?lang=en)

The underlying geospatial archive includes more than 17,000 raster layers covering the period from 1984 to the present at global extent and 1 km spatial resolution. These datasets are accessible through:

- FAO Agro-Informatics Platform
- Image Services (WMTS)
- ArcGIS Online
- Google Earth Engine (GEE)

## Further Information

For more information, please visit the [GIEWS Earth Observation website].(https://www.fao.org/giews/earthobservation/index.jsp?lang=en)

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Country Guidelines for the GSNmap initiative (FAO, 2022), which provide technical specifications for generating national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. The guidelines describe standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions, with outputs including soil nutrient levels as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity. These products support evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en

The reference evapotranspiration dataset is provided at approximately 10 km spatial resolution globally, using different climate data sources for both historical and future periods.

Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020.

For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.

The reference evapotranspiration dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Resources theme and Moisture Regime sub-theme.

For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) evaluates the current vegetation health in comparison to the historical trends.  The VCI relates current dekadal Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) to its long-term minimum and maximum, normalized by the historical range of NDVI values for the same dekad. The VCI was designed to separate the weather-related component of the NDVI from the ecological element. 

                                           
𝑉𝐶𝐼𝑖=(𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑖−𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑚𝑖𝑛) / (𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑚𝑎𝑥−𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑚𝑖𝑛)

Together with Temperature Condition Index (TCI), Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) is used to calculate Vegetation Health Index (VHI) using formula: VHI=0.5*VCI+0.5*TCI

In ASIS, VCI is computed in two modality: dekadal and monthly. The dekadal/monthly VHI raster layer published in FAO Agro-informatics Platform/GEE/ArcGIS Online is further updated in the following 5 dekads (improve data precision, remove cloud pixel etc.).

Non-seasonal indicators (NDVI anomaly, VCI and VHI) provide alternative measures of vegetation health. These indices measure vegetation conditions relative to historical norms rather than in absolute terms and can be used to monitor the areas where vegetation may be stressed. A high value indicates that vegetation is healthier or less stressed than is typical for that location and time of year, while a low value implies the opposite. For example, a high value in a sparsely vegetated environment, such as a savannah, reflects above-average vegetation performance for that setting, not dense or lush vegetation.

We recommend that users rely primarily on ASIS seasonal indicators (ASI, Drought Intensity and Weighted Mean VHI) for agricultural monitoring. If significant discrepancies with local conditions are observed in the seasonal indicators, these are likely due to limitations in the crop phenology and/or crop mask data. In such cases, users may wish to refer to the non-seasonal vegetation indicators. Please visit GIEWS Earth Observation website FAQs (https://www.fao.org/giews/earthobservation/faq.jsp?lang=en) for further information.

Flags of raster file: 251=missing, 252=cloud, 253=snow, 254=sea, 255=background

For further information, please visit FAO GIEWS Earth Observation website at: https://www.fao.org/giews/earthobservation/index.jsp?lang=en

dataIdentification.purpose: FAO Global Information and Early Warning System on Food and Agriculture (GIEWS) monitors the condition of major foodcrops across the globe to assess production prospects. To support the analysis and supplement ground-based information, GIEWS utilizes remote sensing data that can provide a valuable insight on water availability and vegetation health during the cropping seasons. In addition to rainfall estimates and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), GIEWS and FAO's CBC Division have developed the Agricultural Stress Index (ASI), a quick-look indicator for the early identification of agricultural areas probably affected by dry spells, or drought in extreme cases. The ASI dissemination system was online in 2014.

The VCI was designed to separate the weather-related component of the NDVI from the ecological element. 

                                           
𝑉𝐶𝐼𝑖=(𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑖−𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑚𝑖𝑛) / (𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑚𝑎𝑥−𝑁𝐷𝑉𝐼𝑚𝑖𝑛)

Together with Temperature Condition Index (TCI), Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) is used to calculate Vegetation Health Index (VHI) using formula: VHI=0.5*VCI+0.5*TCI

In ASIS, VCI is computed in two modality: dekadal and monthly. The dekadal/monthly VHI raster layer published in FAO Agro-informatics Platform/GEE/ArcGIS Online is further updated in the following 5 dekads (improve data precision, remove cloud pixel etc.).

Non-seasonal indicators (NDVI anomaly, VCI and VHI) provide alternative measures of vegetation health. These indices measure vegetation conditions relative to historical norms rather than in absolute terms and can be used to monitor the areas where vegetation may be stressed. A high value indicates that vegetation is healthier or less stressed than is typical for that location and time of year, while a low value implies the opposite. For example, a high value in a sparsely vegetated environment, such as a savannah, reflects above-average vegetation performance for that setting, not dense or lush vegetation.

We recommend that users rely primarily on ASIS seasonal indicators (ASI, Drought Intensity and Weighted Mean VHI) for agricultural monitoring. If significant discrepancies with local conditions are observed in the seasonal indicators, these are likely due to limitations in the crop phenology and/or crop mask data. In such cases, users may wish to refer to the non-seasonal vegetation indicators. Please visit GIEWS Earth Observation website FAQs (https://www.fao.org/giews/earthobservation/faq.jsp?lang=en) for further information.

Flags of raster file: 251=missing, 252=cloud, 253=snow, 254=sea, 255=background

For further information, please visit FAO GIEWS Earth Observation website at: https://www.fao.org/giews/earthobservation/index.jsp?lang=en

**Remote Sensing Based Water Productivity Assessment in the Kamping Pouy Irrigation System (KPIS), Battambang, Cambodia**

The WP analyses conducted in Cambodia are intended to support the Irrigated Agriculture Improvement Project; this Project will assist the Government of Cambodia to modernize and improve the climate and disaster resilience of four irrigation systems in Battambang, Kampong Cham, Kampong Thom, and Takeo provinces to supply water to 43,500 hectares. dataIdentification.abstract:
GSOCseq is a country-driven global product which depicts the projected Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) stocks (in t C ha-1) 20 years into the future, in current agricultural lands under different soil management scenarios that vary in the degree of carbon inputs to the soil, at 0-30 depth and 1 x 1 km spatial resolution.

__Initial SOC stocks (GSOCseq_T0_Map030)__
This map represents an estimate of current soil organic carbon stocks (in t C ha-1) in 2020 (stocks at time 0; t0), at a soil depth of 0-30 cm. The best available national datasets collected over the years from the different countries were used to derive the 2020 baseline stocks

__Final SOC stocks under business as usual scenario(GSOCseq_finalSOC_BAU_Map030)__ 
This map represents the projected soil organic carbon stocks (in t C ha-1) in 2040 (t20), after 20 years of business as usual (BAU) management, at a soil depth of 0-30 cm.

__Final SOC stocks under sustainable soil management scenario 1 (GSOCseq_finalSOC_SSM1_Map030)__
This map represents the projected soil organic carbon stocks (in t C ha-1) in 2040, after 20 years of implementation of sustainable soil management (SSM) practices that generate a 5 percent increase in carbon inputs (SSM Scenario 1), at a soil depth of 0-30 cm.

__Final SOC stocks under sustainable soil management scenario 2 (GSOCseq_finalSOC_SSM2_Map030)__ 
This map represents the projected soil organic carbon stocks (in t C ha-1) in 2040, after 20 years of implementation of sustainable soil management (SSM) practices that generate a 10 percent increase in carbon inputs (Scenario 2), at a soil depth of 0-30 cm.

__Final SOC stocks under sustainable soil management scenario 3 (GSOCseq_finalSOC_SSM3_Map030)__
This map represents the projected soil organic carbon stocks (in t C ha-1) in 2040, after 20 years of implementation of sustainable soil management (SSM) practices that generate a 20 percent increase in carbon inputs (Scenario 3), at a soil depth of 0-30 centimeters.

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

lineage.statement:
1) Methodology. A crop mask was produced using a supervised classification analysis was carried out for Malanje, Bié and Huambo in Angola using a Random Forest model. 

2) Preprocessing: Sentinel-2 data is preprocessed using Sen2Cor for atmospheric correction and cloud masking. The time series is then gap-filled and resampled to 10-days from January to May 2024.

3) In-situ: The in situ data set shared by GGPEN to conduct the pilot study are spread over 3 different years (2019, 2020 and 2021). Most of the points are from 2020. In 2019 and 2020, the points are spread over the 3 provinces while in 2021, the points are all included in the Bié province. The insitu data for the three years was used to generate a cropland mask.4) Validation: Due to the absence of validation data, only a visual analysis of the product can be done. This analysis shows that most of the pixels identified as cropland do correspond to cropland in reality, but that the product suffers from significant commission error. Errors are mostly located in the areas where the in situ data density is lower.

Class - Caption

1 - Crop

2 - No crop

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

citation.title: Land Cover South Laos (2009)

dataIdentification.abstract: This land cover database has been produced after the Ketsana Typhoon that hit Laos in September 28, 2009. Land cover monitoring and assessment is essential for the sustainable management of natural resources, environmental protection, food security, and of course for measuring the impact and extent of natural disasters. Commissioned by the Lao FAOREP, the GIS and RS group of the FAO NR Department has conducted a quick interpretation of historical satellite imagery (Landsat ETM from the Global Land Survey archive), dated around 2000, according to procedures, methodologies and tools established by the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme. The LCCS approach was adopted to classify the land cover.

otherConstraints: This work is made available under the [Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/)

dataIdentification.purpose: Main goal of this product is to provide a general understanding  of location and distribution of main land cover types, especially related to agricultural production and infrastructure, in order to broadly estimate the extent and impact of the flooding, and provide decision makers information on prioritization of rehabilitation activities.

lineage.statement: Landsat satellite images (ETM), dated around 2000, were selected for the area. (8 scenes). Given the purpose of this data set, which is to support analysis post-typhoon in flooded lands, the area of interest was defined using a buffer zone of 20 km from the main streams. For each scene, band 4, 3 and 2 were extracted in order to produce a false colour composite which enhances the detection of vegetation coverage. MADCAT software (from the GLCN tools set, http://www.glcn.org/sof_0_en.jsp), was used to delineate polygons and assign labels according to an ad hoc land cover legend, which was generated using the Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) software. When completed the interpretation of all scenes, an edge matching process and a topological consistency check was conducted. The table of attributes was also completed with all land cover information provided by an LCCS-based classification.

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was made available online as part of the SOIL+ project, sponsored by AFACI. The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GloSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Global Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration Potential Map (GSOCseq), developed under the Global Soil Partnership to support Sustainable Development Goal Indicator 15.3 on land degradation neutrality. The GSOCseq map follows a country-driven bottom-up approach, where national SOC sequestration maps are produced and validated by local experts using standardized SOC models and the best available data. These products provide an evidence base for assessing soil restoration potential and supporting sustainable land management policies. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cb2642en

The map represents the water deficit per pixel computed as 1 minus the ratio of ETa over ETx (max crop ET) over the Samba main growing season (August to December) 2017, for the irrigated command areas identified by the ADB project in Tamil Nadu state of India.

The RWD50 image indicates pixels showing up to 50% water deficit. The pixel value in the RWD50 indicates the percentage of time (no. of deficit days/total days in a season) a given pixel experienced up to 50% of the water deficit.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The Global Soil Nutrient and Nutrient Budget Maps (GSNmap) is an initiative under the Global Soil Partnership that provides national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. Following the Country Guidelines (https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en ), it uses standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions. Outputs include soil nutrient as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity, supporting evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development.

This particular dataset was produced under the SOIL+ project, sponsored by the Asian Food and Agriculture Cooperation Initiative (AFACI, https://www.rda.go.kr/afaci/site/project/view?). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GloSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

organization.description:
The Land and Water Division (NSL) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has developed a platform to support global and national-level drought monitoring. The global platform provides access to curated datasets and analytical tools designed to characterize drought vulnerability.  The platform integrates authoritative datasets across a people, land, and water framework, enabling governments, development practitioners, financial institutions, and research communities to identify drought-prone areas, assess risk, and prioritize targeted responses. The tool is intended to serve as part of an iterative process of drought monitoring, response, and mitigation.  The methodology is globally consistent while allowing for country-specific contextualization to reflect local conditions and needs.
Datasets span four key vulnerability dimensions (environmental, infrastructure, economic, and social) and are relevant to sectors including water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), agriculture & livestock, energy, environment, and inland navigation. They are available for viewing and download on an individual basis. In addition, analytic tools are available to collectively assess vulnerability across dimensions and datasets.
Developed in collaboration with CIMA Research Foundation.

Static snapshots of wosis_latest are released at irregular intervals for consistent citation purposes and to discuss methodological changes; the last snapshot is available at https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-4735-2024.

dataIdentification.abstract:
This land cover data set is derived from the original raster based Globcover regional (Africa) archive. It has been post-processed to generate a vector version at national extent with the LCCS regional legend (46 classes). This database can be analyzed in the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG), which provides a user-friendly interface and advanced functionalities to breakdown the LCCS classes in their classifiers for further aggregations and analysis. 

The data set is intended for free public access. 

The shape file's attributes contain the following fields:
-Area (sqm)
-ID
-Gridcode (Globcover cell value)
-LCCCode (unique LCCS code)

You can download a zip archive containing:
-the shape file (.shp)
-the ArcGis layer file with global legend (.lyr)
-the ArcView 3 legend file (.avl)
-the LCCS legend tables (.xls)
dataIdentification.supplementalInformation:
This land cover product is a vector version (ESRI shape) of the Globcover archive that was published in 2008 as result of an initiative launched in 2004 by the European Space Agency (ESA). Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) datasets on land cover globally. Given the need of this valuable information for environmental studies, natural resources management and policy formulation, through activities of the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme, the Globcover has been reprocessed to generate databases at national extent that can be analyzed through the Advanced Database Gateway software (ADG) by GLCN. ADG is a cross-cutting interrogation software that allows the easy and fast recombination of land cover polygons according to the individual end-user requirements. Aggregated land cover classes can be generated not only by name, but also using the set of existing classifiers. ADG uses land cover data with a Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend.
The ADG software is available for download on the GLCN web site at [FAO Openknowledge](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b6dfe2d5-1e1b-4511-800b-cc6f872e0378/content).
dataIdentification.purpose: Land cover  is extremely important for natural resource assessment and management, environmental modeling and decision-making. Given that the Globcover is currently the most recent (2005) and resoluted (300 m) global dataset on land cover, the Global Land Cover Network (GLCN) programme has promoted the processing of this database to make it complaints with the GLCN standards and usable through its tools set for land cover based analysis and modelling.

lineage.statement: This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

**Data lineage:**

This land cover database is provided as ESRI shape file (vector format) and derives from reprocessing the raster based Globcover database (regional version). Globcover has undergone the following process: a) vectoralization at the national extent using ESRI ArcGis (arcinfo) 9.3; b) topological reconstruction (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); c) simplification of areas according to a minimum mapping unit of 0.1 skim (10 ha) (custom AML scripts launched inside ArcGis-arcinfo 9.3); application of the FAO/UNEP Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) legend (46 classes); final processing to assure full compatibility with the GLCN software Advanced Database Gateway (ADG).

AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

citation.title: Agro-ecological attainable yield for current cropland (Global - 20 years average - ~1 km) - GAEZ v5

dataIdentification.abstract:
Agro-ecological attainable yield results represent average attainable yield values for current cropland as indicated in the GAEZ v5 land cover inventory for 2020, expressed as Kg (DW)/ha, with a spatial resolution of approximately 1 km. They account for both rain-fed and irrigated conditions, as well as two different levels of input management (high and low). Results are provided for more than 70 major crops including traditional and adapted crops in alignment with the Vision for Adapted Crops and Soils (VACS) [(see Appendix 4-1 of the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation)](https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki/14.-Appendix-4%E2%80%901-Crops), and cover all land and soil groups identified in the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD v2) (FAO & IIASA, 2023). 

For most crops the yields are given in kg dry weight per hectare. For sugar beet and sugar cane the yields are in kg sugar per hectare and for oil palm in kg oil per hectare. Cotton yields are given as kg lint per hectare. Note that for comparison of statistical production (usually in harvested/fresh weight) with GAEZ simulated potential production (yield calculated mostly as dry weight of main produce) an appropriate conversion factor must be applied. Technical coefficients used to convert to fresh weight are included in the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation.

Agro-ecological attainable yield  is estimated using different climate data sources for both historical and future periods.
Historical climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program, covering the periods 1981–2000 and 2001–2020.
For future projections, climate model outputs from the latest CMIP6 IPCC AR6 are used, based on three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.c Pathways (SSPs) and spanning four time periods: 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100.

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Suitability and Attainable Yield theme and Suitability Index sub-theme.

For additional information on the data contained in this dataset, please see the [(readme file)](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/9d36fa97-6272-4307-b81a-3a9a663357b1/resource/ae45310c-8b7e-4c84-8644-341e4c126c85/download/_readme_res05.xlsx). For more detail on the GAEZ v5 methodology, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The Global Soil Nutrient and Nutrient Budget Maps (GSNmap) is an initiative under the Global Soil Partnership that provides national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. Following the Country Guidelines (https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en ), it uses standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions. Outputs include soil nutrient as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity, supporting evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development.

This particular dataset was produced under the SOIL+ project, sponsored by the Asian Food and Agriculture Cooperation Initiative (AFACI, https://www.rda.go.kr/afaci/site/project/view?). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GloSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The annual P/PET ratio time series dataset is provided at approximately 10 km spatial resolution globally, spanning from 1980 to 2022. Climate data is sourced from AgERA5 from the Copernicus program.

The ratio (%) compares the amount of incoming precipitation to the evaporative demand of the reference crop assumed in the calculation of the Penman-Monteith equation used for reference evapotranspiration ETo. An index value of 100% means that precipitation equals reference potential evapotranspiration, i.e. that precipitation on average over the year matches the evaporative demand of the vegetation. Values below 100% indicate the occurrence of some water deficit; values above 100% mean that precipitation exceeds evaporative demand on an annual basis.

The annual P/PET time series dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Agro-climatic Resources theme and Moisture Regime sub-theme.

For additional information, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).
