citation.title: Downscaled harvested area (Global - 2020 - ~10 km) - GAEZ v5

dataIdentification.abstract:
Results on harvested area for the year 2020, are provided in hectares at a global scale with approximately 10 km spatial resolution for 38 major crops/crop groups [(see Appendix 4-1 of the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation)](https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki/14.-Appendix-4%E2%80%901-Crops), separately in rain-fed, irrigated or total cropland. Country totals are based on FAOSTAT statistics for the years 2019-2021 (accessed in 2022).

For single crops or fairly homogenous crop groups (other cereals, yams and other roots) the units of production are in 1000 ha (as used in FAOSTAT). For crop groups which include a greater variety of crops (i.e., vegetables, stimulants) international price weights compiled by FAO (constant 2014-2016 I$) were used to aggregate individual items.

This dataset is part of the GAEZ v5 Actual Yields and Production theme and Area, Yield and Production sub-theme.

For additional information on the data contained in this dataset, please see the [(readme file)](https://data.apps.fao.org/catalog/dataset/febec0c6-dcf1-4897-8003-0b627cdd21bb/resource/1fa9d9f9-ffd0-49d3-b11f-65bb3b04590e/download/_readme_res06.xlsx). For more detail on the GAEZ v5 methodology, please refer to the GAEZ v5 Model Documentation (accessible at https://github.com/un-fao/gaezv5/wiki).

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.

dataIdentification.abstract:
The Harmonized World Soil Database version 2.2 (HWSD v2.2), developed by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), is a global soil inventory providing information on the morphological, chemical and physical properties of soils at approximately 1 km (30 arc-second) spatial resolution. Its main objective is to support biophysical modelling, agroecological zoning and assessments related to food security and climate change.

HWSD v2.2 builds on previous versions of the database (HWSD v1.2, v2.0 and v2.01), incorporating improvements in data coverage, soil attribute information, classification and harmonization. The database integrates global, regional and national soil inventories and provides soil properties for seven standard depth layers (0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80, 80–100, 100–150 and 150–200 cm), replacing the two-layer structure of HWSD v1.2. It includes an expanded range of soil attributes, such as effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC), total nitrogen, carbon-to-nitrogen ratio (C/N) and aluminium saturation.

Soil units are classified according to the FAO 1990 Revised Legend and correlated with the World Reference Base for Soil Resources (WRB 2022). Soil attribute values are derived from the WISE30sec database, which also provides the associated statistical information.

HWSD v2.2 addresses data gaps and inconsistencies identified during the development and application of the Global Agro-Ecological Zoning assessment (GAEZ v5). It includes corrections to soil data and soil phase information, updated WRB soil classifications, and revised procedures for estimating rootable soil depth and available water capacity (AWC), resulting in a more complete and consistent database for global and regional agroecological and environmental assessments.

A full description of the database, its methodology and the changes introduced in version 2.2 is provided in the accompanying technical report (Nachtergaele et al., forthcoming).

lineage.statement:
HWSD v2.2 is the latest in a series of releases: HWSD v1.2 (FAO et al., 2012), HWSD v2.0 (FAO and IIASA, 2023) and the HWSD v2.01 update. Each release has kept the same 30 arc-second raster framework, in which every grid cell is linked to a soil mapping unit described by a soil association.

The spatial component was compiled from the FAO/UNESCO Digital Soil Map of the World, regional and national Soil and Terrain (SOTER) databases, the European Soil Database and national soil inventories. These sources differ in scale, date and classification. They were reconciled into a single legend based on the FAO 1990 Revised Legend, and a correlation to WRB 2022 was added in v2.0.

In v2.0, soil attribute data previously derived from the ISRIC-WISE database were replaced with estimates from WISE30sec (Batjes, 2015). This increased the number of soil profiles used from approximately 10 250 to 21 000. The new attribute data allowed the vertical structure to be extended from two layers (0–30 and 30–100 cm) to seven layers reaching 200 cm, and new soil properties to be added.

The revision to v2.2 was triggered by gaps, errors and inconsistencies identified during the development and application of GAEZ v5. Soil phase information missing from areas covered by SOTER and SOTER-WISE-derived (SOTWIS) databases was completed using the FAO/UNESCO Digital Soil Map of the World. The phases were transferred by spatial overlay of the source inventories and assigned to the dominant soil units within each soil association. Erroneous soil phase information in the European Soil Database coverage was reviewed and corrected. WRB 2022 classifications were then reassessed to reflect the corrected phases. Finally, rootable soil depth and available water capacity were recalculated following the GAEZ v5 methodology (van Velthuizen et al., 2026).

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

This dataset relates to the Country Guidelines for the GSNmap initiative (FAO, 2022), which provide technical specifications for generating national maps of soil nutrients and associated properties at 250 m resolution. The guidelines describe standardized digital soil mapping procedures to ensure consistency and comparability across countries and regions, with outputs including soil nutrient levels as well as key soil properties such as organic carbon, pH, texture, bulk density, and cation exchange capacity. These products support evidence-based agricultural planning and policy development. To cite or share: https://doi.org/10.4060/cc1717en

dataIdentification.abstract:
The land cover map of Tunisia, highlighting cultivated land, olive trees, dates and orchards while integrating information on land water management practices. A land cover map was derived using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery and after stratified with water management data from currently existing data. Statistics illustrating the area of each class regionally and nationally were produced to provide accurate information on land cover classes distribution.

The 2022 land cover map of Tunisia served as an input dataset for the crop suitability assessment of wheat, barley, olive, and date palm, carried out within the framework of the SoLaWiSE initiative following the Agro-Ecological Zoning methodology (see attached report).

organization.description:
AQUASTAT collects, analyses and disseminates data and information, by country, on water resources, water use and agricultural water management, with emphasis on irrigated agriculture in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Its goal is to support agricultural and rural development through sustainable use of water and land by providing the most accurate information presented in a consistent and standard way.

What AQUASTAT offers:

__Standardized data and information__: To provide you with evidence to measure progress and to substantiate your decisions

__Tools__: To allow you to generate your own analysis and conclusions, articles and presentations

__Capacity development__: To improve your understanding and monitoring of water resources, uses, and irrigation management.

Concretely, this means that we provide data, metadata, reports, country profiles, river basin profiles, regional analyses, maps, tables, spatial data, guidelines, and other tools on:

* Water resources: internal, transboundary, total
* Water uses: by sector, by source, wastewater
* Irrigation: location, area, typology, technology, crops
* Dams: location, height, capacity, surface area
* Water-related institutions, policies and legislation.

dataIdentification.abstract:
This dataset was developed under the AFACI project - Development of the Soil Atlas of Asia and National Soil Information Systems (2019-2023). The project supported AFACI member countries in collecting, harmonizing, and managing national soil data to strengthen evidence-based decision making for sustainable soil management. Activities included rescuing legacy soil data, harmonizing national soil maps for the Soil Atlas of Asia, building national soil profile databases and soil property maps, and establishing web-based soil information systems. The project fostered regional and international collaboration, promoted soil data sharing, and contributed to the Global Soil Information System (GLOSIS) under the Global Soil Partnership.

organization.description:
The Land and Water Division (NSL) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has developed a platform to support global and national-level drought monitoring. The global platform provides access to curated datasets and analytical tools designed to characterize drought vulnerability.  The platform integrates authoritative datasets across a people, land, and water framework, enabling governments, development practitioners, financial institutions, and research communities to identify drought-prone areas, assess risk, and prioritize targeted responses. The tool is intended to serve as part of an iterative process of drought monitoring, response, and mitigation.  The methodology is globally consistent while allowing for country-specific contextualization to reflect local conditions and needs.
Datasets span four key vulnerability dimensions (environmental, infrastructure, economic, and social) and are relevant to sectors including water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), agriculture & livestock, energy, environment, and inland navigation. They are available for viewing and download on an individual basis. In addition, analytic tools are available to collectively assess vulnerability across dimensions and datasets.
Developed in collaboration with CIMA Research Foundation.

organization.description: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) have cooperated over several decades to develop and implement the Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) modelling framework and databases. AEZ relies on well-established land evaluation principles to assess natural resources for finding suitable agricultural land utilization options. It identifies resource limitations and opportunities based on plant eco-physiological characteristics, climatic and edaphic requirements of crops and it uses these to evaluate suitability and production potentials for individual crop types under specific input and management conditions. Managing the constraints imposed by agro-ecological conditions and knowing what the most viable crop options are, facilitates planning decisions. In this way choices can be made, which are not only more productive, but also sustainable and resilient to climatic variability. The AEZ framework contributes to several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by providing information about current and future agricultural production risks and opportunities, irrigation water demand, and crop development and adaptation options.
